title: "Second derivatives: forward over reverse"

`cppODE()` computes Hessian-vector products of a scalar functional
$\mathcal{J}(\theta)$ of the solution, such as the objective function of a fit, by
differentiating the reverse sweep in forward mode. Symbols are those of
the [notation table](methods-overview.html#notation). R interface:
`derivMode = "forward-reverse"` of [`cppODE()`](../reference/cppODE.html)
and `cotangent`, `tangent` and `curvature` of
[`solveODE()`](../reference/solveODE.html).

## Hessian-vector products

For a fixed cotangent, [Reverse (1)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-contraction)
defines the gradient map
[]{#eq-gradient-map}
$$
  \bar\theta : \mathbb{R}^{M} \to \mathbb{R}^{M},
  \qquad \theta \mapsto \nabla_\theta \mathcal{J}(\theta), \tag{1}
$$
with Jacobian $\nabla^2_\theta \mathcal{J}$. The sweep evaluating
[(1)](#eq-gradient-map) is generic in the scalar type. On
$\mathtt{dual}\langle\mathtt{double}\rangle$ with $N$ tangent slots,
seeded with $V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$, it returns the exact
$(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{J},\; \nabla^2_\theta \mathcal{J}\,V)$ [@pearlmutter1994fast];
$V = I_M$ gives the Hessian. For an ODE this is the second-order adjoint
[@wang1992second; @ozyurt2005cheap]. The result `curvature`, of shape
$[n_x + n_p, N, n_{\text{seed}}]$, comes with the `cotangent` and
`tangent` of the same run.

## Second-order adjoint system

For a direction $v = (v_0, v_p)$, the directional sensitivity $\sigma$
solves [Forward (1)](methods-forward.html#eq-sensitivity-p) contracted
with $v$,
[]{#eq-soa-tangent}
$$
  \dot\sigma = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\sigma
             + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\,v_p,
  \qquad \sigma(t_0) = v_0, \tag{2}
$$
and the tangent $\mu$ of $\lambda$ along $v$, the derivative of
[Reverse (2)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-ode), runs backwards from
$\mu(T^+) = 0$,
[]{#eq-soa-adjoint}
$$
  \dot\mu_i = -\sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_i}\,\mu_k
            - \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
                \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
              + \sum_m \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial p_m}\,v_m
              \right), \tag{3}
$$
with jumps $\mu(t_o^-) = \mu(t_o^+) + \dot w_o$, $\dot w_o$ the
derivative of the cotangent row $w_o$ along $v$, zero for a cotangent
independent of $\theta$. A cotangent formed from the solution, such as a
weighted residual, passes $\dot w_o$ as the `curvature` argument, an
array $[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_x, n_{\mathrm{seed}}, N]$; without it the
Hessian misses the dependence of the cotangent on $\theta$, the gradient
not. Differentiating
[Reverse (5)](methods-reverse.html#eq-adjoint-quadrature) along $v$ gives
the state half $\mu(t_0)$ of $\nabla^2_\theta \mathcal{J}\,v$ and the parameter
half
[]{#eq-soa-quadrature}
$$
  \int_{t_0}^{T}\left(
      \sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial p_m}\,\mu_k
    + \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
        \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
      + \sum_l \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial p_l}\,v_l
      \right)\right)\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4}
$$

cppDE does not integrate [(2)](#eq-soa-tangent) to
[(4)](#eq-soa-quadrature); the dual instantiation gives their discrete
counterpart. The tangent of $\lambda$ is $\mu$ on the forward grid, the
tangent of the parameter accumulator is [(4)](#eq-soa-quadrature). The
second derivatives of $f$ in [(3)](#eq-soa-adjoint) and
[(4)](#eq-soa-quadrature) come from $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and
$(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ over duals, so the
first-order sweep needs no further generated expression. For a Rosenbrock
method these include the contractions of $J v$, second derivatives of
$f$.

## Cost and memory

The sweep reads tangents from the checkpoints, so the forward pass is a
sensitivity run in the same $N$ directions. A checkpoint holds
$(q+1)\,n_x (N+1)$ numbers; memory is linear in the number of steps. The
error test and first step of the forward pass include the tangents by
`sensErrCon` (default `TRUE`); with `sensErrCon = FALSE` the grid does
not depend on the directions. The cost, one sensitivity integration and
one sweep of width $N$, is linear in $N$. A difference quotient of the
gradient would cost $N$ gradient evaluations and lose half the digits.

| | forward over forward | forward over reverse |
|:--|:--|:--|
| argument | `derivMode = "forward-forward"` or `deriv2 = TRUE` | `derivMode = "forward-reverse"` |
| result | `hessian`: every state, every parameter pair | Hessian of one functional |
| cost | quadratic in $M$ | lower by a factor $M$ for a likelihood |
| use | state Hessians (only route); any functional by contraction | Hessian of a likelihood |

## Linear solves and tangent storage

The matrix of a Rosenbrock stage has tangents, so the transposed solve
applies the implicit function theorem with the transposed matrix
(`cppde_ad_lu.hpp` dense, `cppde_sparse_ad_lu.hpp` sparse). The
iteration matrix of a `bdf` or `adams` corrector has none: the sweep
solves against it on values, with the tangents as further right-hand
sides. Under `bdf` the sweep solves the corrector equation ([Adjoint of
the step map](methods-reverse.html#adjoint-of-the-step-map)) with a
stopping test on the values, so every block of directions takes the same
iterations. A generated model body releases on return the tangent
storage it allocated, so the sweep binds the tangent storage of every
buffer before passing it to the model, as the stepper does for internal
buffers.
